Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on February 20, 2025
Review Body: I watched the movie first. Being a voracious reader I immediately purchased the book for my kindle. (The book is always better than the movie). The language in this book surprised me at first. I’ve never known hillbillies maybe they do cuss up a storm! I was raised poor. My father passed at age 29. My Mom had to go to work to support us. Her parents were dead. In the 1950’s there were no social services or programs to help! I never heard a curse word until high school. JD Vance’s turning around his life circumstances is nothing short of Miraculous! I throughly enjoyed this read. And the insight it gives our now Vice President of the United States is also amazing to understanding. It is comforting to know real people are in charge in the White House! By that I mean honest people we can trust!

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on August 11, 2024
Review Body:
What amazed me most was how quickly I was able to borrow and read this book on my Kindle via Libby. I live in Brevard County FL, which is about 60% pro-Trump. I was able to borrow immediately, and renew immediately. Noone waiting on it, less than two weeks after Trump's announcement of his VP choice. The man is running for VP of the USA, less than 9 years after finishing Yale Law School, and et noone in my county but me was interested in reading about him.
So, I lived in Appalachian Georgia for almost 35 years. With different names and places, I know these people, families, and their lives. Vance's analysis is generally comprehensive, nuanced, and I tend to agree with most of his conclusions. My only real complaint is his very weak understanding of the constraints on women's lives in the 40s to 60s before reliable forms of birth control became available.
Absolutely recommended reading. Then, like me, you can wonder about this man.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on August 6, 2024
Review Body:
Five Stars⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐For some reason, Goodreads won't allow me to rate this book either through Kindle or on the Goodreads app.
This is a well written, sincere story about a modern American Dream come true despite several setbacks, tribulations and loss. It's a love story about the strength of family and support to come through struggles and break unhealthy patterns.

In a lot of ways, there are similarities with Dr. Ben Carson's story with his mother's love and value of education and a loving wife to build a strong family life. Although, in Vance's case, his grandparents, particularly his Mamaw, gave his strong guidance to overcome life struggles.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on August 2, 2024
Review Body:
This memoir has been on my list for a while and I finally read it after it was announced that JD Vance is the VP candidate alongside Trump.

I have seen criticism of it based on the "hillbilly" term with many suggested he isn't one. In this day and age, I think he has a right to claim that title if he so chooses.

That aside, in the afterword Vance explains he had two questions he hoped to answer through writing this memoir:

#1 "Why does this elite institution seem so culturally foreign?" - he was referencing Yale Law Schhol

#2 "Why are so few kids who grow up as I did - 'disadvantaged,' to use the vocabulary of the day - making it to our society's elite institutions."

I think he did a good job answering those questions throughout the telling of his life story.

Vance is an interesting man. I admire that he enlisted in the service and used that experience to help him through college and eventually law school.

I bought the Kindle version of this book. I also borrowed the audio from my library. Vance narrates the audio and does a good job of it.

Review Body:

His main conservative idea is that those who work shouldn’t have to pay to keep up those who don’t. It will be interesting to observe what he says in the 2024 presidential campaign.

He pays scant deference to Christianity, but is not hostile to it. If he is ever characterized as a “conservative Christian” that would be doubly misleading.

It seems that his description of the “hillbilly” personality could perhaps more aptly be applied to “white trash”.

I bought the paperback because it was much cheaper than the Kindle. It’s the first time in quite a while I’ve read a printed book. There’s no reason I’d want to re-read it.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on July 21, 2024
Review Body:
No doubt the language stopped me at first, then I thought - it is the language of the place and time. It reminded me of a lady visiting from New Jersey who was cussing her son during a time when I was interviewing her for a newspaper story. She said, "Sorry about the language but this is the way we talk back home. If we really don't like somebody there is probably a gun or knife involved." So don't let the foul words stop you from reading Hillbilly Elegy - for the messages within its pages are too important to miss.

The book is well written or well spoken should I say as I listened to it on my Kindle. The time of a child, teenager and young adult written so as to identify real challenges in life that are just what they are... It made me think that children are born into circumstances that they did not define, and many times they reach a fork in the road and take a path others might not have, or follow the crowd. Vance, the author, articulates circumstances that many may not ever see unless they do so through his well versed paragraphs that become chapters.

I would suggest you read Hillbilly Elegy with an open mind... It might give you a different look at why society is shaped the way it is today; why some make it and others don't. It also might give you a glimmer of hope as you look toward the future.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on July 21, 2024
Review Body:
The most interesting parts of Vance's book dealt with the difficulties Vance encountered as the son of an alcoholic/addict mother, and his relationship with his grandparents. The fact that his grandparents were hillbillies is not really so important, although there are quite a few amusing anecdotes about this. I have to respect Vance for enduring and excelling under such difficult conditions, although his remarkable grandparents deserve much of the credit. The book probably should have stopped there.

The parts dealing with his stint in the Marines I found pretty boring and predictable, and the same with his time at Ohio State. The sections in which he expands on the decline of his hometown of Middletown Ohio were not very well-written, as if they had been added in a rush. For example, he criticizes the young men of the town for not working more than 20 hours per week, and in effect calls them lazy. A few paragraphs later he says that factors other than laziness might be at play, such as lack of work opportunities. Later on, he again calls them lazy.

Also, Vance assumes a poverty-ridden neighborhoods are crime-ridden neighborhoods, which is not necessarily true. Moreover, it's difficult to tell when he is presenting poverty statistics for the current Middletown as opposed to the Middletown he experienced as a child. I was left with the feeling that Vance might be either trying to make his childhood success story more interesting by magnifying the level of hardship in his town, or he was in a haste when writing.

I had had enough when I reached the 67% marker on the Kindle, so I can't say much more.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on May 29, 2019
Review Body: I’m interested in memoirs in general but after seeing J.D. on Tucker Carlson and hearing how strong and eloquently he gave his educated opinion, I knew I had to read his book! I’m also partial to military veterans and whatever they have to say about their perspective on war and politics. I could not put the book down! Or rather, my phone, since I have the kindle edition. I would not have believed, listening to him speak today, that he came from a background like the one he details in the book. Without giving too much away, his type of childhood and lack of parenting does not normally produce a man of his caliber, character and educational acumen. It still blows my mind three weeks after finishing the book that someone can endure these hardships and constant letdowns and rise up through the ashes to become a “wildest dreams” version of themselves. It really proves what is possible for those who WANT change and are willing to work their butts off to accomplish their goals. He talks about very key people in his life who helped him, loved him, guided him but it’s really his effort and determination that got him to where he is. Now I’m nagging my children about this guy and telling them what they can do if they put their minds to it but sadly, their lives are too devoid of strife and chaos to really care. In other words, they have the perfect life with normal parents who love and protect them and that my friends, is ideal and awesome but KILLS any fire and NEED to rise above. A JD Vance would not be born of an easy-peasy life. Telling someone to work hard for everything they want isn’t the same thing as having no other option. That’s why I love this book so much. It inspires you! And, he’s just a really freaking good writer that gets to the point in a gut wrenching way. You SEE the town he’s talking about in your minds eye. You HEAR his raunchy gramma spouting profanities right in front of him and yet, being astute enough to know when to give hugs and praise. You will feel uplifted, inspired, proud, angry, frustrated and victorious all throughout this book but you will never regret or forget!

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on March 5, 2019
Review Body:
I love to read memoirs not only to learn about how others live, but to learn what they've learned. I so wanted to love this book, and in the beginning I liked it. But by the time I got to about 55% to 60% per my Kindle, I just couldn't read anymore. The other night I thought I'd jump to the last chapter and just see if I could glean some bit of wisdom or perspective. No such luck.

This book is disorganized, wordy, and repetitive. I was confused as to the timeline of his life most of the time. When I got to the part where he recounted all his moves by year in school, I thought to myself (or maybe even said out loud), "If you'd told the story well up to this point, you wouldn't have to recap all of this now." He should have read a few books on memoir writing before he embarked on his first draft. Then he would have known that just because it happened doesn't mean it's interesting or advances the story.

I also found it strange that he attributed terminology that's used in many parts of the country to being "hillbilly" words. For example "crawdad" he says has hillbilly origins. But that's what we called them in Southern California when I was a kid. I did a poll on Facebook and found that almost all of my FB friends who answered called them crawdads, too. Except the one from Pennsylvania.

And what is his overarching point? I'll never know. He didn't reveal it in the 70% of the book I managed to slog through, and I'll never be able to bring myself to finish it. It's unfortunate, because I'm sure there are lessons from his life that readers would benefit from.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on January 31, 2019
Review Body:
One of my bestest recently read J.D. Vance’s HILLBILLY ELEGY: A MEMOIR OF FAMILY AND CULTURE IN CRISIS for a graduate course that she is taking, and she asked me if I’d ever read it. Shockingly, I hadn’t. I started the book that very night and I said to myself: “what took you so long,” as it was sitting idle on my Kindle for who knows how long. Surely, you’ve heard of it. Bill Gates loved it. As clearly did the other hundreds of thousands who read it.

The book is outstanding. Not always easy to digest. Not due to any fault of the author’s. Rather because of the nature of what he goes through. You will get past these issues and you must. That is what makes it so astounding.

It’s the true story of Vance’s childhood and young adult life, growing up in the Rust Belt, after moving with his family from Kentucky to Ohio. His father is not part of his life. His drug-addict mother seemingly does the best she can for young J.D. and his caring older sister, while their mother moves on from husband to husband in rapid succession. But it is the grandparents who take care of him and leave the most lasting impression. They ensure that he is loved, have food on the table, get an education, and learn that the only way out and up is to aspire beyond a factory job.

Vance’s story is triumphant. His writing will move you to laughter, to tears, and beyond anything you can imagine. He paints a picture of more obstacles than one person should have to hurdle in a lifetime. Yet, watch him leap.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 16, 2018
Review Body:
When Hillbilly Elegy finally made it off my list and onto my Kindle, I was really excited to dig in, even though I wasn't sure what to expect.

I think J.D. Vance's motivation and purpose is admirable. The story, at times, is really interesting, driven unequivocally by the author's fantastic grandmother. I could have read a story solely about her. As this was written, toward the end, I found myself skipping pages, as it felt repetitive and ultimately just ran too long and lost me.

The book walks a line - at times it feels like a story and at other times it feels like more of a textbook study on Appalachia. Because of this, Hillbilly Elegy lacks a bit of cohesiveness.

For me, this read came right after I finished Tara Westover's book, Educated, a book written in a similar vein and is a tough act to follow.

Despite that criticism, there's also a lot that shines here: J.D. brings humor, sorrow, and some tales from his life that are downright harrowing.

There are a lot of folks, not just the poor from Appalachia, who can really benefit from J.D.'s message. His story, the path he took despite his origins, is quite amazing. I'm glad he chose to share his experiences with us.

Go Bucks.

Review Body: Having grown up in southern Ohio, I found his story compelling, but wish that I had waited for it to go down in price. $12 for the Kindle edition was not worth it. The structure was chaotic, like his life, and he repeated a lot of his personal history. I should have done a better job of researching before buying, but was in a hurry. I was expecting more of a sociological examination of the history, culture, and problems of the Appalachian folk. It was more of an autobiography of a kid who grew up as "white trash" with dysfunction and disruption. He should be proud that he managed to work hard and succeed with the help of his bat-shit crazy, but loving and protective, Grandma. I didn't come away with any more of an understanding of the particular Hillbilly cultural pathology that causes so much misery among these people. My people came to hillbilly southern Ohio from northern Ohio and were not embraced because we were Catholic, Italian Americans. The Hillbilly folk are tribal and clannish. This seems to be their major downfall from my perspective. The movie might be good, but I won't pay to see it in the cinema, will wait for Netflix.

Review Body:
I got this book because I’ve been fascinated and appalled that Donald Trump ran for President and won, when he’s obviously a gangster and a lousy businessman. He should have been in jail for hanging out with gangsters while he ran casinos -- very illegal, and much more, plus he managed to stay in business despite a billion dollars debt because he illegally money laundered Russian mafia money. Nor didTrump didn’t tell all the banks he'd borrowed from about his other outstanding loans, again, illegal, so the banks let him stay in business since he’d still be making some revenue and shutting him down meant writing off a billion dollars. And much more...

Anyone who’d read the book The Making of Donald Trump would have known all this. Or if the media had covered his past. But the media focuses on what is happening RIGHT NOW, which was mostly Trumps latest outrageous tweets. Of course, who can blame them, the public wants infotainment, not news, and to stay in business, that's what newspapers and TV offer for the most part.

Having read a lot about Trump before the election, I was sure the voters would elect Hillary Clinton, and consequently threw the worst party ever on election night. We didn’t get to drink any of the half dozen bottles of champagne.

Ever since I’ve sought out books explaining who Trump voters are and why they voted for him. A search on “books about why people voted for Trump” often includes Hilllbilly Elegy.

But this book Elegy should not be on the list. It’s just another memoir of growing up in a dysfunctional family and culture. He can’t touch the misery of The Glass Castle: A Memoir or A Long Way Gone: Memoirs of a Boy Soldier . There are no insights about why hillbillies went from voting Democratic to becoming right-wing Republicans, and often evangelical Christians who’d like to replace America’s laws with Biblical Commandments. Blacks and Hispanics grew up in equal if not greater poverty, but they didn’t go that direction.

For that, you’ll want to read Joe Bageant’s orders-of-magnitude better book “deer hunting” from 2008. It’s far more brilliant and fun to read, plus full of insights you may have never come across before. Instead of dwelling on his family only, he also paints vivid portraits of other working class people he grew up with before escaping with a college scholarship. To see if you’d like to read it, I have some kindle notes and analysis at energyskeptic post “Book Review of Deer Hunting with Jesus”.

If you want to understand how hillbilly culture began and why it’s different from other dysfunctional poverty stricken groups, then White Trash: The 400-Year Untold History of Class in America is the book for you. “White Trash” goes back to the founding of the U.S. and beyond to the Calvinist Scots-Irish immigrants who came here. It will be a shocking book to many who haven’t read much history, because it shows why and how it came to be that Americans have never been equals, and never will be.

If you want to understand why the white working class went from being Democrats to Republicans, read “ One Nation Under God: How Corporate America Invented Christian America ” or for a summary, search from my post “How corporations used conservative religion to gain wealth and power and undo the New Deal” at energyskeptic.

What nobody writes about is the deeper reason poverty keeps growing. We’ve hit the limits to growth, the peak of energy and natural resources, with a still exponentially growing population who will want stuff. Both both Republicans and Democrats offer the solution of “growing our way out of it”. Obviously, on a finite planet, infinite growth isn’t possible. Bageant knows this, but doesn’t dwell on it. I know he knows because mentions James Howard Kunster, the writer most similar to Bageant I can think of, especially his books The Long Emergency: Surviving the End of Oil, Climate Change, and Other Converging Catastrophes of the Twenty-First Century and The Geography of Nowhere: The Rise and Decline of America's Man-Made Landscape

To read my kindle notes search on energyskeptic and Hillbilly Elegy. Since the excerpts are yanked from various parts of the book, there’s no narrative flow, but it may give you an idea of whether you like his writing enough to purchase the book. If you like hard luck memoirs that may be enough reason.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on July 28, 2017
Review Body:
The outcome of the election made me want to better understand how Donald Trump was able to appeal to middle America. After reading this book, I get it. This former marine and Yale Law School graduate provides a probing look at the struggles of America’s white working class through the author’s own story of growing up in a poor Rust Belt town. This is an especially fascinating book and a must read. It gives us a peek into the 21st century lives of some stubborn, fearless folks in Eastern Kentucky who do not assimilate well into the larger society. It really helped me after the election of Trump to better understand why so many workers no longer identified with the Democratic Party and how desperate they were to find an alternative political option. The author provides examples and quantifiable, sociological analysis on how extensive the gap between the wealthy and poor continues to grow in the US.

The fact is J.D. Vance has written a revealing book about his childhood life in the hillbilly subculture of impoverished Eastern Kentucky and parts of southern Ohio. One of his goals is to describe for the reader why the people of Eastern Kentucky have not been able to break out of poverty, why generation after generation of children in this subculture follow the behavioral patterns set by their parents and neighbours when these patterns of behaviour have not greatly improved the education of their people nor their economic condition in the larger society.

The moving memoir has its share of humour and introduces us to a number of vividly colourful figures. It is the story of how upward mobility really feels as well as being an urgent and troubling meditation on the loss of the American dream for an ever growing segment of the country.

It is very obvious after reading it why 'Hillbilly Elegy: A Memoir of a Family and Culture in Crisis' by J.D. Vance has been on the NY Times Best Seller List for over a year now. This touching, revealing, warm, sad, and inspiring memoir, opens many sores while explaining in the most human and personal terms possible the pain and misunderstanding that harms working class and poor white Americans in the heartlands.

Throughout, Vance painstaking honesty and courage are never in doubt. Ultimately, Vance fully understands the necessity for a compassionate government and individual acceptance of responsibility working together to make progress possible for all. I found it so fascinating I've bought the hardback when it was originally released and have now bought the kindle edition to store and reference back to. A must read.
I am a verified purchaser in Australia

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on July 13, 2017
Review Body:
Hillbilly Elegy: A Memoir of a Family and Culture in Crisis by J.D. Vance (Harper Collins, 2016, $12.59/15.99) has been on the NY Times Best Seller List for forty-nine weeks, and at the time of this writing, stands at number two. This touching, revealing, warm, sad, and inspiring memoir, written by a Yale Law School graduate whose childhood was spent in the hills of eastern Kentucky and the migrated community of Middletown, OH, opens many sores while explaining in the most human and personal terms possible the pain and misunderstanding that harms working class and poor white Americans in the Hheartlands. Throughout this tale Vance sometimes mentions findings of academic studies and other research, using them to support or introduce his own poignant experiences, but, most of all, this is the story of one man's ability to persevere in an environment where success such as he has experienced is rare, and , according to him psychically costly as well as economically expensive.

Living within a home with serial father figures coming and going and an alcoholic, drug addicted mother, he attributes the source of his core values to life in rural Jackson, Kentucky in the hills and hollers of Appalachia with his Mamaw and any number of uncles and cousins. He describes on academic paper in which the authors suggest that “hillbillies learn from an early age to deal with uncomfortable truths by avoiding them, or by pretending better truths exist, a characteristic of bluegrass music, too. Vance refuses to look the others way.

Vance tracks the two major migrations from Appalachia to the industrial mid-west, particularly Middletown, OH, which were mirrored in the South, mid-South and New England, the depression era migrations and the post-WWII migration of returning veterans. He examines how the regions prospered and then died off with the decline of America industrial might, leaving abandoned neighborhoods, unemployment, and drug dependency behind, attributing this to both bad government policies and globalism.

Vance consistently refers to himself and his family as being poor and then at other times being “working class.” Joan C. Williams, in White Working Class seems to make a clear distinction between the two while Vance vacillates. He talks about “his people,” Kentucky migrants to southern Ohio, as often living off the dole, not working, and being plagued by drugs and violence, yet also talks about an uncle who escapes to the middle class, and his mother who, despite being an addict, was a nurse who was able to work a good deal of the time. He glories, however, in his extended family, his many uncles who provide him with male role models in both positive and negative ways. At times he seems remarkably judgmental, while at others, forgiving.

As Vance matures through adolescence, he begins to see the disjointures between both liberal and conservative points of view. He sees many of the government programs as well meaning but ineffective while the conservative solutions were disciplinary and draconian. In his reading of sociology, while in high school, he began to realize that the situation of black people described in his readings about black America contained the same dilemmas as did the lives and existence of the white working poor from Appalachia. “Our Elegy is a sociological one, yes, but it is also about psychology and community and culture and faith.” (144) He's writing about religion, work, and family when he observes the deep “cognitive dissonance between the world we see and the values we preach.” (147)

As Vance prepares to attend Yale Law School he explains in touching, no-holds-barred language why a person like him, growing up in poverty, bedeviled by the rigors of having a drug addicted mother living with multiple husbands, and seemingly inured to violence and loss could reject the attractions of both the left and the right. These chapters, presented within the context of an actual life lived in poverty and difficulty, if not despair, bring so many working class and poor white men, especially, to accept so much patently untrue or misleading material in seeking to understand who they are, why they got that way, and how difficult it is to extricate oneself. In short, Vance asserts, it's easier for many to blame “the other” than it is to do the hard analysis of one's own choices, accept the verdict, and get to work to change things. What sets J.D. Vance apart is his ongoing optimism, despite all evidence to the contrary.

Interestingly, Hillbilly Elegy can also stand as a “How To” book for those seeking to find their own way to a different place in both the workplace and in society. For instance, the non-verbal behavioral cues of social class are significantly different than the behaviors that pass for progressing in working class employment and social environments. Vance shows himself always to be exceptionally alert to what's going on around him. As he gains in self confidence, his ability to ask questions of those he trusts increases. He's also a very fast learner. Nevertheless he owns to deep feelings of abandoning the culture from which he comes while yearning to become part of that with which he's not, yet, thoroughly familiar. However, the struggle is neither easy nor always successful.

Throughout Hillbilly Elegy: A Memoir of a Family and Culture in Crisis, Vance scatters data and information from relevant sociological and psychological writing to illuminate the points he makes, to give them a solid theoretical context. Such use of accurate research information never seems intrusive or fault-finding. Rather, it seeks to help a reader generalize from the highly personal revelation of the pain and confusion of Vance's childhood. It helps the reader gain understanding and perspective without ever excusing either those who raised him or his own mis-understandings, missed paths, and possibly botched relationships. He bravely opens the scars on his psyche, examines them, faces their consequences, and comes out the other side a stronger and better person. His painstaking honesty with the reader and his courage are never in doubt. This is not a book for the reader to quarrel with. Rather, it requires being good listeners, seeking to find the truths as they apply to them. Some would prescribe better, more effective programs. Others view the problems of poverty and drug addiction as the fault of the victim. While, ultimately, Vance looks towards personal responsibility for life, he fully understands the necessity for a compassionate government and individual acceptance of responsibility working together to make progress possible for all. I bought the book and read it on my Kindle app.

If having a dysfunctional family and rising above by joining the marines and going to law school before you lose the peach fuzz on your face means you should write a memoir of your life so far, I know a lot of people sitting on a lot of money.

3. J.D Vance is not a good writer or storyteller. His stories and antidotes that he has coming out of his poor Memaw (did we really need pronunciation guides for 'Memaw" JD? Come on.) are so common and I heard them growing up so much in Virginia that I stared to think that I may be a hillbilly, twice removed. Who knew??

Review Body:
I found Hillbilly Elegy (Kindle Version) an interesting and engaging read. It brings one face-to-face with the struggles of that around 13% of the population that live in poverty and the many more who live near the poverty line. While it focuses on the experiences of the descendants of the immigrants who populated Appalachia and, later, the rust belt, the takeaways can be extrapolated to the larger swath of America that faces economic struggles. The author touches on quantitative and qualitative reasons for this populations’ particular struggle with economic mobility, with the main themes being a loss in confidence in the American Dream, failed familial relationships, and lack of exposure to the possibilities that are reserved for the upper and upper-middle class. This book is a particularly topical given the recent election and focus on the growing inequality in America.

What made this work better than an economic paper on the rise of inequality is the author’s personal experience with the struggles that are faced by a large swath of our society. I found this aspect of the book the most appealing. The author credits idiosyncratic reasons for his ability to escape this environment. He does not give many policy prescriptions for the treatment of ills that plague his community, nor does he portend to, but he does lay much blame at the feet of his community. While I have similar political leanings to the author, his prognosis seems inconsistent with his own experiences. Claiming he made it out by sheer luck and supportive grandparents, it is unclear how he would have done this under different circumstances through hard work, which he claims is a lost value in his community. This is underscored other places in the memoir where he claims ignorance in the ways of the upper class, such as etiquette and networking. The latter, he says, is the most important way to make it ahead. I also did find it unusual that while he diagnoses these problems, he did not describe becoming significantly involved in any effort to be that example of success that his community so sorely lacked.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 31, 2016
Review Body: I borrowed this book from my library and read it on my Kindle, which means that I did not pay the full Kindle price to read it, and I appreciate my library for that. First, as a story, I found this book interesting and entertaining. I conclude that JD Vance is not a hillbilly at all. Nor is his mother a hillbilly. It seems that his biological father is. However, JD was born in Ohio, as was his spoiled mother. Both he and his mother had a middle class, if not “f***** up” life there. His grandparents were the hillbillies before they moved to Ohio. This is like me claiming all the characteristics and identity of my grandparents when in fact my life was totally different from theirs. JD has an affinity, but not the true identity. On the subject of his mother, she seems to exhibit borderline personality disorder. His childhood was very difficult. Although I was raised poor, and there was alcohol, my parents stayed together and were loving, and that made a big difference. Talking to my daughter on the phone today about the book, she pointed out to me that I and my husband, her dad, caused her a lot of harm and she was probably more abused than her own husband, whose parents we accuse of being bad. A difference from JD’s mom is that both my husband and I stayed married, were not histrionic, and worked our whole lives. We were drug addicts and/or alcoholics for a few years and snapped out of it. Luckily. True confessions all too common in the milieu of American middle-class families, not so funny. I think it is a pop culture phenomenon that this book has made it to the best sellers list. I’m disappointed to hear that JD is working for Peter Thiel at his financial firm. That seems like a big waste of JD’s talent. I suppose he just wants to make a lot of money. In spite of my criticism, I can’t help admire the pluck and energy of JD Vance. I still think the book is worth reading because it is a pop culture phenomenon, basically. I like to read best sellers. Color me shallow.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 29, 2016
Review Body:
“There is a cultural movement in the white working class to blame problems on society or the government, and that movement gains adherents by the day.” (Kindle Locations 2630-2631)

“There is no group of Americans more pessimistic than working-class whites.” (Kindle Locations 2641-2642).

Close-minded, skeptical of progress, suspicious of change, and ready to brand anything or anyone new or different as ‘foreign’ and unwanted; the culture of southeastern Kentucky—but for, sadly, the introduction of drugs to the mix—doesn’t seem to have changed much in more than sixty years.

Reading J. D. Vance’s, Hillbilly Elegy: A Memoir of a Family and Culture in Crisis, has almost convinced me that I might have been a more perceptive sixteen year old than I’d ever credit myself with being. I remember that the brief time I spent in the rural, Lily/London, region of that state, in 1957, was an incredible culture shock to this New England/New York city kid. I think it would still be, today. It is still a culture in crisis, and now it seems be angry, too.

J.D. Vance’s journey from the deep poverty of a hillbilly hollow in Kentucky to law school at Yale put me in mind, somewhat, of Esmeralda Santiago’s (When I Was Puerto Rican) trip from poverty-stricken, rural, Puerto Rico to a Harvard education. The odds are incredible, almost insurmountable, and the accomplishments in both instances, heroic. But far too few escape the chaos.

Recommendation: Smacks of cultures and attitudes we might despair of, but do well to know more about. Hillbilly Elegy is a story for today.

“Chaos begets chaos. Instability begets instability. Welcome to family life for the American hillbilly.” (Kindle Location 3070)

HarperCollins. Kindle Edition, 257 pages.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on November 4, 2016
Review Body: Like the author, I too am a product of an Eastern Kentucky mountain family. Like his family and neighbors, my relatives and friends were poor working class folks surrounded by other families in like circumstances. But, beyond that, our childhood experiences couldn't have been more different. For example, I never heard my grandmother (or anyone else in my household or the household of my friends) use gutter language, and I never witnessed violence in my home or in any other home. My father had a gun but he never pointed it at a human being and he certainly never threatened anyone with it. I've come to the conclusion that Mr. Vance is blaming Appalachia for his family's plight while ignoring their lack of common decency and self-discipline. The real culprits for the dysfunction he experienced in his early life were his family members, not the area of the country that spawned them. Update: I see the Kindle version is now $14.99. I thought it was a rip-off at $5.29.
